title: Networking & Linux Security Foundations
why: You can't secure what you don't understand. This module builds the same foundational networking and Linux knowledge every security professional needs, framed from day one around defense: knowing how systems work so you can recognize when something is wrong and know how to harden it.

topics.title: Ethics and scope — the rule that comes first
topics.concept: Before any technical content: security skills are powerful, and using them against systems you don't own or have EXPLICIT WRITTEN AUTHORIZATION to test is illegal in virtually every jurisdiction — the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (US) and equivalent laws elsewhere treat unauthorized access as a crime regardless of intent. This entire path teaches DEFENSIVE understanding and AUTHORIZED testing practice (your own local lab, sanctioned CTF/Capture-The-Flag competitions, or a real engagement with a signed authorization). Every concept from here forward is taught for that purpose — understanding a vulnerability class to defend against it, never to exploit systems you don't have permission to touch.
topics.analogy: A locksmith learns how locks work, including their weaknesses, specifically so they can help people secure their homes — practicing lockpicking on YOUR OWN lock, or a client's lock with their explicit permission, is a legitimate skill. Picking a stranger's lock without permission, even 'just to see if it works,' is a crime regardless of how curious or well-intentioned you are. Security skills follow the exact same line.

examples.code:
# The authorization checklist before ANY security testing, always
authorization_checklist = [
    "Do I own this system, OR",
    "Do I have EXPLICIT WRITTEN permission from the owner, OR",
    "Is this a sanctioned platform built for practice (e.g. a CTF, a designated training lab)?",
    "If none of the above are true: STOP. Testing this system is not authorized.",
]
for item in authorization_checklist:
    print(item)
examples.note: This is the mental checklist every security professional runs before touching ANY system, every single time -- 'I was just curious' or 'I didn't cause any real damage' are not legal defenses for unauthorized access in essentially any jurisdiction.

topics.warn: This module and the rest of this path deliberately do NOT provide exploit payloads, real attack scripts targeting live systems, or step-by-step 'how to break into X' instructions. All hands-on practice should happen against your own local machine, your own deliberately-vulnerable practice environments (like OWASP's own training platforms, referenced in later lessons), or sanctioned CTF competitions — never against a system you don't have explicit permission to test.
mistakes: Assuming 'no real harm done' or 'I told them afterward' makes unauthorized access legal — it generally does not, under laws like the CFAA.
Testing against a live production system 'just to check' without explicit written authorization — even well-intentioned bug-hunting on systems you don't own can constitute a real crime.

Treating this path's defensive framing as a limitation rather than the actual professional standard — real, employed security professionals overwhelmingly work defensively and under strict authorization; that IS the job, not a watered-down version of it.
topics.handsOn: Write down, in your own words, the three legitimate contexts where security testing is authorized (your own systems, explicit written permission, sanctioned practice platforms). Then identify one platform (research this yourself — e.g. a well-known CTF platform or an intentionally-vulnerable training app) you could practice on legally once you have hands-on skills later in this path.
topics.doneWhen: You can clearly state the authorization boundary for security testing and name at least one legitimate, sanctioned practice context.

checks.q: Is it legal to test a website's security 'just to see if it's vulnerable' if you don't own it and haven't been given permission?
checks.a: No — unauthorized access or testing, even without malicious intent or actual damage, is generally illegal under laws like the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (US) and equivalent laws elsewhere. Authorization must be explicit (ownership, written permission, or a sanctioned practice platform) before any testing.

keyTakeaways: Security testing requires explicit authorization: ownership, written permission, or a sanctioned practice platform.
Unauthorized access is illegal regardless of intent or whether damage occurred.
This entire path teaches defensive understanding and authorized practice — the actual professional standard.

topics.title: Core vocabulary: the CIA triad and AAA
topics.concept: The CIA TRIAD names the three properties nearly every security control ultimately protects: CONFIDENTIALITY (only authorized parties can read the data — protected by encryption), INTEGRITY (data hasn't been tampered with — protected by hashing and digital signatures), and AVAILABILITY (the system stays usable for legitimate users — threatened directly by attacks like DDoS, and protected by redundancy/rate-limiting). AAA names the three related but distinct steps controlling WHO can do WHAT: AUTHENTICATION (proving who you are — a password, a token, an SSH key), AUTHORIZATION (checking what that verified identity is actually allowed to do — an access-control rule), and ACCOUNTING (recording what actually happened — logging, for later audit or incident investigation). These six terms aren't new mechanisms — you'll recognize the underlying techniques from other lessons in this path — but naming them explicitly is exactly the vocabulary a security interview or certification expects you to use precisely.
topics.analogy: The CIA triad is what every lock, seal, and backup generator on a building is ultimately protecting: confidentiality is the locked door (only the right people get in), integrity is a tamper-evident seal on a package (you'd know if it was opened), availability is the building's backup generator (it stays open even when the main power fails). AAA is the building's front desk process: authentication checks your ID, authorization checks whether your badge actually opens THIS specific door, and accounting is the sign-in log recording who came through and when.

examples.code:
# Mapping CIA + AAA onto mechanisms already covered in this path (not new code -- a vocabulary map):
# Confidentiality -> symmetric/asymmetric encryption, TLS/HTTPS      (Cryptography Fundamentals module)
# Integrity       -> hashing, digital signatures                     (Cryptography Fundamentals module)
# Availability    -> DDoS defenses, redundancy, rate-limiting        (this module's DDoS lesson)
# Authentication  -> passwords, MFA, SSH keys                        (Web Security: cyber-auth-secrets)
# Authorization   -> access-control checks, least privilege          (cyber-web-broken-access-control, cyber-cloud-iam-least-privilege)
# Accounting      -> logs, audit trails                               (Security Operations: cyber-log-analysis)
examples.note: This is a deliberate vocabulary map, not new code to run -- the point of this lesson is recognizing that mechanisms you've already learned (or will learn later in this path) are each answering one of these six named questions, which is exactly the framing a security interview expects.

mistakes: Being able to explain a mechanism (e.g. 'hashing detects if a file changed') without knowing which CIA property it maps to (integrity) -- interviewers and certification exams routinely ask for the term, not just the mechanism.

Confusing authentication with authorization -- proving who you are (authentication) is a completely separate check from what you're allowed to do once verified (authorization); a valid, authenticated user can still be correctly denied a specific action.

Treating accounting as an afterthought -- without logs, a security incident can't be investigated after the fact at all; accounting is what makes 'what actually happened' answerable, not just 'what should have happened.'
topics.handsOn: For each of the 6 terms (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability, Authentication, Authorization, Accounting), write one sentence naming a specific real-world example of a control that protects/implements it -- at least 2 should reference something covered elsewhere in this path.
topics.doneWhen: You can define all six CIA/AAA terms without notes, and correctly map at least 4 of them to a specific mechanism you've learned.

checks.q: A system correctly identifies a user via their password (authentication succeeds), but then blocks them from deleting another user's account. Which AAA property is doing the blocking, and how does it differ from authentication?
checks.a: Authorization. Authentication only verifies WHO the user is; authorization is the separate check for WHAT that verified user is actually allowed to do. A user can be correctly authenticated and still be correctly denied a specific action they're not authorized for.

keyTakeaways: CIA triad: Confidentiality (encryption), Integrity (hashing/signatures), Availability (DDoS defenses, redundancy) — the three properties security controls ultimately protect.
AAA: Authentication (who you are), Authorization (what you're allowed to do), Accounting (what actually happened, via logs) — three distinct, sequential checks.
These are vocabulary for mechanisms you already know or will learn — naming them precisely is what a security interview or certification specifically expects.

topics.title: How networks actually work
topics.concept: Every network connection follows the same basic pattern: an IP ADDRESS identifies a machine (like a street address), and a PORT identifies a specific SERVICE on that machine (like an apartment number) — port 80/443 for web traffic, port 22 for SSH remote access, port 53 for DNS. Understanding what's normally running on which ports is foundational to BOTH offense and defense — a defender who doesn't know their own system's normal open ports can't recognize an abnormal one.
topics.analogy: If an IP address is a building's street address, ports are the individual apartment numbers within it — mail (network traffic) addressed to '192.168.1.10, apartment 22' goes specifically to the SSH service, not the whole building. A security-conscious building manager knows exactly which apartments are supposed to be occupied (which ports SHOULD be open) — so an unexpected new occupant (an unexpectedly open port) immediately stands out as worth investigating.

examples.code:
# Common, well-known ports (memorize these -- they come up constantly in security work)
well_known_ports = {
    20: "FTP (data)", 21: "FTP (control)",
    22: "SSH (secure remote login)",
    23: "Telnet (INSECURE remote login -- avoid)",
    25: "SMTP (email sending)",
    53: "DNS (domain name resolution)",
    80: "HTTP (unencrypted web)",
    443: "HTTPS (encrypted web)",
    3306: "MySQL database",
    5432: "PostgreSQL database",
}
for port, service in sorted(well_known_ports.items()):
    print(f"port {port:>5}: {service}")
examples.note: This is a reference table worth genuinely memorizing -- recognizing that port 23 (Telnet) being open on a modern system is an immediate red flag (it transmits credentials in PLAIN TEXT, unlike SSH's port 22) is a real, practical security-awareness skill, not just trivia.

examples.code:
import socket

def check_port(host, port, timeout=1):
    sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    sock.settimeout(timeout)
    result = sock.connect_ex((host, port))   # 0 means the port is open/reachable
    sock.close()
    return result == 0

# Checking YOUR OWN localhost -- always authorized, since it's your own machine
for port in [22, 80, 443, 3306, 9999]:
    status = "open" if check_port("127.0.0.1", port) else "closed"
    print(f"localhost:{port} -- {status}")
examples.note: This checks ports on 127.0.0.1 (localhost) -- YOUR OWN machine, always a legitimate target for this kind of check. connect_ex returning 0 means the connection succeeded (port open); a non-zero value means it failed (closed/filtered). This exact technique, run against someone else's system without authorization, is a form of network scanning that requires permission -- the ethics lesson's boundary applies here directly.

mistakes: Running the port-check example (or any network scanning tool) against a host you don't own or have permission to test — even a 'harmless' check is scanning, and scanning without authorization can itself be a violation.
Confusing an IP address (identifies the MACHINE) with a port (identifies the SERVICE on that machine) — a very common beginner mix-up.

Assuming an open port is automatically a vulnerability — many open ports are intentional and necessary (e.g. 443 for a real website); the concern is UNEXPECTED or misconfigured open ports, not open ports in general.
topics.handsOn: Run the port-check example against your own localhost (127.0.0.1) and confirm the results match what you know is actually running on your machine. Memorize the well-known ports table — you'll need this vocabulary throughout the rest of the path.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain the IP-address-vs-port distinction, name at least 5 well-known ports and their services, and have safely checked your own localhost's port status.

checks.q: Why is port 23 (Telnet) considered a security red flag on a modern system, while port 22 (SSH) is standard and expected?
checks.a: Telnet transmits data — including login credentials — in PLAIN TEXT over the network, meaning anyone intercepting the traffic can read them directly. SSH encrypts the connection, protecting credentials and data in transit, which is why SSH replaced Telnet as the standard for secure remote access.

keyTakeaways: An IP address identifies a machine; a port identifies a specific service on that machine.
Knowing which ports SHOULD be open on your own systems is foundational to recognizing abnormal activity.
Scanning ports on a system you don't own or have permission to test is a form of unauthorized activity — only test your own systems or authorized targets.

topics.title: Linux file permissions and hardening basics
topics.concept: Linux security starts with its permission model: every file has three permission sets (owner/group/other), each controlling READ, WRITE, and EXECUTE access, commonly shown as a string like `-rwxr-xr--` or a number like `754`. The PRINCIPLE OF LEAST PRIVILEGE — giving a file, process, or user only the access it genuinely needs, nothing more — is the foundational hardening idea underneath almost every Linux security practice, from file permissions to service accounts to firewall rules.
topics.analogy: Linux file permissions are like a building with three tiers of keys: your OWN office key (owner), a shared department key (group), and a general lobby key anyone in the building might have (other). The principle of least privilege says: don't hand out master keys to everyone just because it's convenient — give each person exactly the access their actual job requires, so a stolen or compromised key (or account) only opens what it was ever supposed to.

examples.code:
import os
import stat

# Create a test file in a safe temp location and inspect its permissions
test_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "perm_test.txt") if "__file__" in dir() else "perm_test.txt"
with open(test_path, "w") as f:
    f.write("test")

mode = os.stat(test_path).st_mode
print("permission string:", stat.filemode(mode))
print("octal:", oct(mode)[-3:])

os.chmod(test_path, 0o600)   # owner read/write ONLY -- no group/other access
print("after chmod 600:", stat.filemode(os.stat(test_path).st_mode))

os.remove(test_path)
examples.note: chmod 0o600 grants read+write to the OWNER only, with zero permissions for group or other -- exactly the least-privilege pattern for a sensitive file (like one containing credentials or private keys), which is why files like SSH private keys are REQUIRED to have restrictive permissions or SSH itself will refuse to use them.

examples.code:
# The permission digits, decoded (this is worth memorizing)
permission_bits = {
    7: "rwx (read+write+execute)",
    6: "rw- (read+write)",
    5: "r-x (read+execute)",
    4: "r-- (read only)",
    0: "--- (no access)",
}
print("chmod 754 means:")
print("  owner:", permission_bits[7])
print("  group:", permission_bits[5])
print("  other:", permission_bits[4])
examples.note: Each digit in a chmod number (like 754) independently sets owner/group/other permissions using the same 3-bit encoding (4=read, 2=write, 1=execute, summed) -- 7=4+2+1=rwx, 5=4+1=r-x, 4=read-only. This decoding is genuinely useful to have memorized rather than looked up every time.

topics.warn: Run these examples on a REAL Linux system (WSL, a Linux VM, or a Linux server) — Windows' NTFS filesystem does NOT implement true Unix permission bits, so os.chmod() on native Windows silently has no real effect (the file stays fully readable/writable by everyone regardless of the chmod value). This is a genuine, verified platform difference, not a hypothetical caveat — always verify Linux-permission code on an actual Linux environment. Also: only create/modify files you own in a safe location — never run permission-modifying commands (chmod, chown) on system files you don't understand, especially with elevated privileges (sudo).
mistakes: Using overly permissive settings (like 777, granting everyone full access) 'to make an error go away' instead of diagnosing the real permission need — a very common, genuinely dangerous shortcut.
Confusing read/write/execute on a DIRECTORY (execute means 'can enter/traverse it', not 'can run it as a program') with the same bits on a FILE (execute means 'can run it as a program').
Running chmod/chown with sudo on system files without understanding the consequence — this can break the system or create real security holes.
topics.handsOn: Run both examples, confirm the permission string and octal notation match, and confirm chmod 600 correctly restricts access. Then create a few test files with different chmod values (644, 700, 755) and predict each one's permission string BEFORE checking it.
topics.doneWhen: You can read and set Linux file permissions in both string and octal notation, and can explain the principle of least privilege in your own words.

checks.q: What does chmod 600 grant, and why is it the correct choice for a sensitive file like an SSH private key?
checks.a: chmod 600 grants read+write to the file's OWNER only, with zero access for group or other users — exactly the least-privilege setting needed for sensitive files, since anyone else with any access to the file could read the private key otherwise.

keyTakeaways: Linux permissions control read/write/execute access separately for owner, group, and other.
The principle of least privilege — granting only necessary access — underlies almost all Linux security hardening.
Overly permissive settings (like 777) as a quick fix for permission errors are a common, genuinely dangerous shortcut.

title: Cryptography Fundamentals
why: Cryptography is the mathematical foundation underneath nearly every other security control in this path — HTTPS, password storage, secure messaging, and code-signing all rest on the concepts this module builds: symmetric vs. asymmetric encryption, hashing vs. encryption (a genuinely different thing), how TLS actually establishes trust, and digital signatures.

topics.title: Symmetric vs. asymmetric encryption
topics.concept: SYMMETRIC encryption uses the SAME key to both encrypt and decrypt — fast and efficient, but both parties must somehow share that secret key beforehand, which is itself a hard problem (how do you securely send the key in the first place?). ASYMMETRIC encryption uses a mathematically-related KEY PAIR: a PUBLIC key (safe to share with anyone, used to encrypt) and a PRIVATE key (kept secret, the only thing that can decrypt) — solving the key-distribution problem, since the public key can be shared openly, but is dramatically slower computationally than symmetric encryption. Real systems (like TLS, covered next) typically use BOTH: asymmetric encryption to securely exchange a symmetric key, then fast symmetric encryption for the actual data.
topics.analogy: Symmetric encryption is like a single physical key that both locks and unlocks a shared lockbox — fast and simple, but you and your correspondent need to have exchanged that exact key beforehand, ideally in person, since intercepting it in transit compromises everything. Asymmetric encryption is like a public mail slot that ANYONE can drop a letter into (the public key, freely shared), but only the box's owner has the one physical key that can actually open it and retrieve what's inside (the private key) — solving the 'how do we exchange the key safely' problem, at the cost of being a slower mechanism than a simple shared key.

examples.code:
from cryptography.fernet import Fernet

# SYMMETRIC: the SAME key encrypts and decrypts
key = Fernet.generate_key()
cipher = Fernet(key)

message = b"transfer $500 to account 12345"
encrypted = cipher.encrypt(message)
decrypted = cipher.decrypt(encrypted)

print("symmetric key (must be kept secret, shared between both parties):", key[:20], b"...")
print("decrypted matches original:", decrypted == message)
examples.note: Actually run and confirmed: the SAME key object both encrypted and decrypted the message correctly. Fernet is a symmetric encryption scheme built on AES -- notice that ANYONE who obtains this one key can both encrypt new messages AND decrypt existing ones, which is exactly the key-distribution problem asymmetric encryption solves differently.

examples.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa, padding
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes

# ASYMMETRIC: a DIFFERENT key pair -- public key encrypts, private key decrypts
private_key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)
public_key = private_key.public_key()

message = b"only the private key holder can read this"
encrypted = public_key.encrypt(
    message,
    padding.OAEP(mgf=padding.MGF1(algorithm=hashes.SHA256()), algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), label=None)
)
decrypted = private_key.decrypt(
    encrypted,
    padding.OAEP(mgf=padding.MGF1(algorithm=hashes.SHA256()), algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), label=None)
)
print("decrypted with PRIVATE key:", decrypted)
print("public_key has a decrypt method at all:", hasattr(public_key, "decrypt"))
examples.note: Actually run and confirmed: decryption with the private key correctly recovers the original message, and hasattr(public_key, 'decrypt') genuinely returns False -- the public key object has NO decrypt capability whatsoever, a concrete, verified demonstration of the one-directional property that makes public-key cryptography solve the key-distribution problem: the public key can only encrypt, never decrypt.

mistakes: Assuming asymmetric encryption is simply 'more secure' than symmetric — they solve DIFFERENT problems (key distribution vs. raw speed); real systems combine both rather than treating one as a strictly better replacement for the other.

Trying to encrypt LARGE amounts of data directly with asymmetric encryption — it's computationally much slower than symmetric encryption, which is exactly why TLS (next lesson) uses asymmetric encryption only to exchange a symmetric key, then switches to symmetric for the actual data.

Confusing 'the public key can be shared with anyone' with 'the public key is not important to protect its INTEGRITY' — if an attacker can trick you into using their public key instead of the real recipient's, they can intercept messages meant for someone else (this is exactly the problem digital certificates, covered next, exist to solve).
topics.handsOn: Run both examples and confirm the symmetric key successfully round-trips a message, and the asymmetric key pair correctly encrypts with the public key and decrypts only with the private key. Then confirm for yourself that trying to call a decrypt-like operation on the public key object fails or doesn't exist.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption, why asymmetric solves the key-distribution problem, and why real systems typically combine both rather than using only one.

checks.q: Why can't you simply share a symmetric encryption key with someone the same casual way you'd share an asymmetric public key?
checks.a: A symmetric key can both encrypt AND decrypt — anyone who obtains it (including an eavesdropper intercepting it in transit) gains full read/write access to anything encrypted with it. An asymmetric public key can only encrypt; even if intercepted, it doesn't grant the ability to decrypt anything, which is why it's safe to share openly while a symmetric key is not.

keyTakeaways: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key for both encryption and decryption — fast, but requires securely distributing that key beforehand.
Asymmetric encryption uses a public/private key pair — the public key encrypts (safe to share), only the private key decrypts, solving the key-distribution problem at the cost of speed.
Real systems (like TLS) typically combine both: asymmetric encryption to exchange a symmetric key, then fast symmetric encryption for the actual data.

Run both examples and confirm the symmetric key successfully round-trips a message, and the asymmetric key pair correctly encrypts with the public key and decrypts only with the private key.

The public key object genuinely has no decrypt capability at the type level, not just 'isn't meant to be used that way' by convention.

topics.title: Hashing vs. encryption — a genuinely different thing
topics.concept: ENCRYPTION is REVERSIBLE by design — with the right key, you get the original data back exactly. HASHING is ONE-WAY by design — there is no key or operation that recovers the original input from a hash; a cryptographic hash function (SHA-256, etc.) also has the AVALANCHE EFFECT: changing even one character of the input produces a completely different, unrelated-looking hash output. This is exactly why passwords are HASHED (you never need to recover the original password, only verify a match) while genuinely sensitive data you DO need back later (like a database's encrypted-at-rest contents) is ENCRYPTED.
topics.analogy: Encryption is like a locked box with a key — reversible by design, since the whole point is getting the original contents back later. Hashing is like putting something through a paper shredder in a very specific, repeatable pattern — you can verify two things were shredded identically (same input, same output), but there's no way to reconstruct the original document from the shredded result. This is exactly why you hash passwords (you only ever need to check 'does this match', never reconstruct the original) but encrypt something like a stored credit card number (you genuinely need the real number back later for a legitimate purpose).

examples.code:
import hashlib
from cryptography.fernet import Fernet

message = "my secret data"

# ENCRYPTION is reversible -- you get the original back with the right key
key = Fernet.generate_key()
encrypted = Fernet(key).encrypt(message.encode())
decrypted = Fernet(key).decrypt(encrypted).decode()
print(f"encrypted then decrypted: '{decrypted}' -- matches original: {decrypted == message}")

# HASHING is one-way -- there is NO operation that recovers the original from the hash
hashed = hashlib.sha256(message.encode()).hexdigest()
print(f"\nsha256 hash: {hashed}")
print("there is no 'unhash' function -- this is fundamentally, mathematically one-way")
examples.note: Actually run and confirmed: the encrypted message correctly round-trips back to the exact original via decrypt(), while the SHA-256 hash is simply a fixed 64-character hex string with no corresponding 'reverse' operation defined anywhere in the hashlib library (or any hash function) -- there genuinely is no way back.

examples.code:
# Confirm: even a TINY change to the input produces a COMPLETELY different hash (avalanche effect)
hashed2 = hashlib.sha256((message + ".").encode()).hexdigest()
print(f"hash of message + one period: {hashed2}")
print("completely different from the original hash, despite a 1-character change --")
print("this 'avalanche effect' is a required property of a cryptographic hash function")
examples.note: Actually run and confirmed: adding a single period to the input produced a hash sharing NO visible resemblance to the original -- this avalanche effect is precisely why a hash can't be 'reverse-engineered' by noticing partial patterns; a tiny, even one-bit change scrambles the entire output unpredictably.

mistakes: Using encryption where hashing is the correct tool (like storing passwords in a reversible, encrypted form) — if you never need the original value back, hashing is the more appropriate, more secure choice, since there's no key to ever compromise and leak the original.

Using hashing where encryption is the correct tool (trying to 'hash' data you'll genuinely need to recover later, like a stored credit card number) — hashing is fundamentally, mathematically irreversible; there's no getting the original back, by design.

Assuming a cryptographic hash is 'basically encryption with an unknown key' — this is a real, common misconception; a proper cryptographic hash has NO key and NO reverse operation, a fundamentally different mathematical property than encryption.
topics.handsOn: Run both examples and confirm encryption round-trips correctly while hashing genuinely has no reverse operation. Then hash a few different, closely-related strings (e.g. 'password', 'Password', 'password ') and confirm each produces a wildly different hash, directly observing the avalanche effect.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain the difference between encryption (reversible) and hashing (one-way), and can correctly choose which one a given real-world scenario calls for.

checks.q: Why are passwords stored as a HASH rather than encrypted (in a reversible form)?
checks.a: A login system only ever needs to verify 'does this match what was stored', never recover the actual original password — hashing is the correct, more secure choice specifically because it's irreversible: even if the hash database is stolen, there's no key or operation that recovers the original passwords from it, unlike encryption which is designed to be reversed with the right key.

keyTakeaways: Encryption is reversible by design (with the right key); hashing is one-way by design, with no operation that recovers the original input.
A cryptographic hash's avalanche effect means even a one-character input change produces a completely different output.
Passwords should be hashed (never needs reversal); genuinely-needed-later sensitive data should be encrypted (needs reversal) — using the wrong one for a given scenario is a real, common mistake.

Hash a few different, closely-related strings (e.g. 'password', 'Password', 'password ', 'password1') and confirm each produces a wildly different hash.

topics.title: TLS and HTTPS — how a browser knows who it's really talking to
topics.concept: HTTPS is HTTP running over TLS (Transport Layer Security), which provides two things: ENCRYPTION (so traffic can't be read in transit) and AUTHENTICATION (proof you're actually talking to the real, intended server, not an impostor) — the second part is what a DIGITAL CERTIFICATE provides. A certificate is issued by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) and cryptographically binds a domain name to a public key; your browser's TLS handshake verifies both that the certificate is signed by a CA it trusts AND that the certificate's domain name actually matches the site you're connecting to — a mismatch (or an untrusted issuer) correctly fails the connection, exactly the defense against an attacker presenting a fake certificate for a domain they don't control.
topics.analogy: Encryption alone (without a verified certificate) is like whispering a secret to someone in a dark room — the message itself might be unintelligible to eavesdroppers, but you have no idea if you're actually whispering to the person you think you are. A verified TLS certificate is like that person also showing you a government-issued ID, checked against a registry you trust (the Certificate Authority) — now you have both privacy (encryption) AND genuine confidence you're talking to the right party (authentication), which is exactly what distinguishes real HTTPS security from encryption alone.

examples.code:
import ssl
import socket

hostname = "www.python.org"
context = ssl.create_default_context()

with socket.create_connection((hostname, 443), timeout=5) as sock:
    with context.wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname=hostname) as ssock:
        cert = ssock.getpeercert()
        print("TLS version negotiated:", ssock.version())
        print("cipher suite:", ssock.cipher()[0])
        print("certificate issued to:", cert.get("subject"))
        print("certificate issued by:", cert.get("issuer"))
        print("valid until:", cert.get("notAfter"))
examples.note: Actually run against the real, live www.python.org: confirmed TLS 1.3 negotiated, a real certificate genuinely issued to 'www.python.org' by a real Certificate Authority (GlobalSign), with a real, currently-valid expiration date -- this is a genuine, live TLS handshake and certificate inspection, not a simulated example.

examples.code:
# Deliberately checking the cert against the WRONG hostname -- should be REJECTED
with socket.create_connection(("www.python.org", 443), timeout=5) as sock:
    try:
        with context.wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname="not-python.example.com") as ssock:
            print("connection succeeded (this would be a real problem!)")
    except ssl.SSLCertVerificationError as e:
        print("Correctly rejected:", str(e)[:100])
examples.note: Actually run: connecting to the real python.org server but asking TLS to verify the certificate against a DIFFERENT hostname genuinely fails with 'Hostname mismatch, certificate is not valid for...' -- this is live proof that certificate verification actively checks the domain name match, and correctly refuses the connection when it doesn't, which is exactly the protection that stops an attacker from using someone else's valid certificate to impersonate a different site.

topics.warn: Never disable certificate verification (e.g. `ssl._create_unverified_context()` or a framework's 'ignore SSL errors' option) in real, production code — doing so silently removes the authentication guarantee entirely, making your connection vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle attack (next module) even though the traffic still LOOKS encrypted.
mistakes: Assuming 'the padlock icon' or 'it's HTTPS' alone guarantees you're talking to the legitimate site — it guarantees encryption AND that SOME certificate was presented and verified for that domain, but doesn't protect against, say, a compromised or maliciously-issued certificate from a CA that shouldn't have issued it (rare, but a real historical failure mode).
Disabling certificate verification to 'fix' an SSL error during development, then forgetting to re-enable it before deploying to production — a genuinely common, serious real-world mistake.

Confusing 'encrypted' with 'authenticated' — traffic can be encrypted between you and an attacker just as easily as between you and the real server; certificate verification is specifically what confirms you're talking to the right party, not just that the channel is private.
topics.handsOn: Run both examples and confirm the real certificate details for a live site, and the hostname-mismatch rejection. Then try the same check against a different real HTTPS site of your choosing, and compare its certificate's issuer and validity period.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what TLS/HTTPS provides (encryption AND authentication), what a certificate binds together, and have verified both a successful and a rejected TLS handshake against a real server.

checks.q: Why does HTTPS need certificate verification in addition to encryption — what would be missing with encryption alone?
checks.a: Encryption alone only guarantees that traffic can't be read by an eavesdropper — it says nothing about WHO you're actually encrypting the traffic with. Certificate verification is what confirms you're genuinely talking to the intended server (via a trusted Certificate Authority's signature and a matching domain name), preventing an attacker from transparently intercepting and relaying traffic while still 'technically' encrypting it.

keyTakeaways: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, providing both encryption (privacy) and authentication (confirming you're talking to the real server) — two genuinely distinct guarantees.
A digital certificate, issued by a trusted Certificate Authority, cryptographically binds a domain name to a public key.
TLS correctly rejects a connection when the certificate's domain doesn't match the hostname being connected to — verified directly against a real server.

topics.title: Digital signatures — proving authenticity, not just privacy
topics.concept: A digital signature does the OPPOSITE key direction from encryption: the SIGNER uses their PRIVATE key to sign a message (producing a signature only they could have created), and ANYONE can VERIFY it using the signer's PUBLIC key — proving the message genuinely came from the private-key holder and hasn't been altered since signing. This is distinct from encryption (which provides privacy) — a signature provides AUTHENTICITY and INTEGRITY, and is exactly the mechanism behind verified software updates, signed commits, and email signing.
topics.analogy: A digital signature is like a wax seal stamped with a uniquely-shaped signet ring that only ONE person owns (the private key) — anyone who sees the resulting seal impression can compare it against a known, publicly-displayed pattern of that ring (the public key) to confirm it's genuine, without needing the ring itself. If even a single word of the sealed letter is altered after sealing, the wax seal breaks visibly — exactly like a digital signature failing verification the instant the signed message is tampered with.

examples.code:
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa, padding
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidSignature

private_key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=2048)
public_key = private_key.public_key()

message = b"this update was genuinely published by the real author"

# SIGNING uses the PRIVATE key -- the opposite direction from encryption's public-encrypts pattern
signature = private_key.sign(
    message,
    padding.PSS(mgf=padding.MGF1(hashes.SHA256()), salt_length=padding.PSS.MAX_LENGTH),
    hashes.SHA256(),
)

# VERIFYING uses the PUBLIC key -- anyone can verify, but only the private key holder could sign
try:
    public_key.verify(
        signature, message,
        padding.PSS(mgf=padding.MGF1(hashes.SHA256()), salt_length=padding.PSS.MAX_LENGTH),
        hashes.SHA256(),
    )
    print("verification (with PUBLIC key): SUCCESS -- signature is genuine")
except InvalidSignature:
    print("verification FAILED")
examples.note: Actually run and confirmed: the signature (created with the private key) verifies successfully using only the public key -- notice signing/verifying uses the OPPOSITE key direction from the earlier asymmetric-encryption lesson (there, the public key encrypted and the private key decrypted; here, the private key signs and the public key verifies).

examples.code:
# Now try verifying a TAMPERED message with the SAME signature -- should FAIL
tampered_message = b"this update was genuinely published by an ATTACKER"
try:
    public_key.verify(
        signature, tampered_message,
        padding.PSS(mgf=padding.MGF1(hashes.SHA256()), salt_length=padding.PSS.MAX_LENGTH),
        hashes.SHA256(),
    )
    print("tampered message verification: SUCCESS (this would be a serious problem!)")
except InvalidSignature:
    print("tampered message verification: FAILED (correctly rejected)")
examples.note: Actually run and confirmed: verification of the ALTERED message with the original signature correctly fails and raises InvalidSignature -- this is live, concrete proof that a digital signature is tied to the EXACT signed content, and any modification after signing (even swapping one word) is detected, which is exactly the integrity guarantee a signature provides beyond just proving who signed it.

mistakes: Confusing digital signatures with encryption — a signature proves authenticity/integrity (who sent it, and that it wasn't altered), while encryption provides confidentiality (that only the intended recipient can read it); a message can be signed, encrypted, both, or neither, depending on which guarantees are actually needed.

Assuming a valid signature alone proves the CONTENT is trustworthy or correct — it only proves the content came from the claimed signer and wasn't altered since signing; the signer themselves could still be lying or wrong about the content's substance.

Losing track of which key does what — remembering 'private key signs, public key verifies' (the reverse of 'public key encrypts, private key decrypts' from the earlier encryption lesson) is a common point of confusion worth deliberately memorizing correctly.
topics.handsOn: Run both examples and confirm the genuine signature verifies successfully while the tampered message's verification correctly fails. Then sign a message of your own choosing, and independently confirm you can identify why the signing key (private) and verifying key (public) are opposite from the earlier asymmetric-encryption lesson.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what a digital signature proves (authenticity and integrity, not privacy), which key signs and which verifies, and have demonstrated real tamper detection with code.

checks.q: In digital signatures, which key is used to CREATE a signature, and which key is used to VERIFY it?
checks.a: The PRIVATE key creates the signature (only the key holder can produce it), and the PUBLIC key verifies it (anyone can check it's genuine) — this is the reverse direction from asymmetric encryption, where the public key encrypts and the private key decrypts.

keyTakeaways: A digital signature is created with the signer's private key and verified with their public key — the reverse direction from asymmetric encryption.
Signatures provide authenticity (proof of who signed) and integrity (proof the content wasn't altered since signing), not confidentiality.
Verifying a tampered message against an original signature correctly fails — directly demonstrated, not just asserted.

title: Network Security & Attacks
why: Module 1 built basic networking literacy — this module builds real network DEFENSE and attack-awareness skills: how firewalls actually decide what to block, why VPNs matter, how a classic man-in-the-middle attack works at the protocol level, and how to scan a network properly and legally, extending Module 1's simple port-check into genuine security tooling.

topics.title: Firewalls and network segmentation
topics.concept: A firewall evaluates traffic against an ORDERED list of rules — the FIRST matching rule wins, and a well-designed firewall ends with a DEFAULT DENY rule (block anything that didn't match an explicit allow) rather than default allow, following the principle of least privilege from Module 1's Linux lesson, now applied to network traffic instead of file access. NETWORK SEGMENTATION takes this further at an architectural level — dividing a network into separate zones (e.g. a public-facing web server segment, isolated from an internal database segment) so that compromising ONE segment doesn't automatically grant access to everything else.
topics.analogy: A firewall's ordered rule list is like a bouncer's specific instruction sheet, checked top to bottom for the first matching instruction: 'if VIP, let in; if on the guest list, let in; otherwise, turn away' — the default-deny final rule is the bouncer's baseline assumption, not an afterthought. Network segmentation is the building itself having separate, badge-restricted floors — a stolen guest badge (a compromised low-privilege segment) doesn't automatically open the executive floor's vault (the isolated, sensitive segment), because the two are physically separated, not just differently labeled.

examples.code:
# A simplified firewall rule engine -- rules are evaluated IN ORDER, first match wins
rules = [
    {"action": "allow", "port": 443, "proto": "tcp", "desc": "HTTPS"},
    {"action": "allow", "port": 80, "proto": "tcp", "desc": "HTTP"},
    {"action": "allow", "port": 22, "proto": "tcp", "desc": "SSH"},
    {"action": "deny", "port": "*", "proto": "*", "desc": "default deny -- block everything else"},
]

def evaluate(port, proto="tcp"):
    for rule in rules:
        port_match = rule["port"] == "*" or rule["port"] == port
        proto_match = rule["proto"] == "*" or rule["proto"] == proto
        if port_match and proto_match:
            return rule["action"], rule["desc"]
    return "deny", "no matching rule (implicit deny)"

for test_port in [443, 22, 3389, 8080]:
    action, desc = evaluate(test_port)
    print(f"port {test_port}: {action.upper()} ({desc})")
examples.note: Actually run and confirmed: ports 443/22 are correctly ALLOWed (matching explicit rules), while port 3389 (RDP -- a commonly-attacked remote-access port when left exposed) and port 8080 both correctly fall through to the DEFAULT DENY rule, since neither has an explicit allow rule -- exactly the default-deny posture a well-designed firewall should have.

topics.warn: Port 3389 (RDP) being blocked by default in this example isn't arbitrary — RDP exposed directly to the public internet is one of the most commonly exploited attack surfaces in real-world ransomware incidents, precisely because it's often left open by default-ALLOW misconfigurations rather than default-deny.
mistakes: Configuring a firewall with a default-ALLOW posture (block only specific known-bad things) instead of default-DENY (allow only specific known-good things) — default-allow requires you to anticipate every possible bad case in advance, which is far less reliable than explicitly allowlisting only what's actually needed.

Treating network segmentation as optional 'extra' hardening rather than a core defense — segmentation is specifically what limits the BLAST RADIUS when (not if) one part of a network is eventually compromised.
Writing firewall rules without considering ORDER — since the first matching rule wins, a broad allow rule placed before a more specific deny rule can silently make that deny rule unreachable.
topics.handsOn: Run the example and confirm the allow/deny results for all four test ports. Then add a new rule allowing port 3389 BEFORE the default-deny rule, and confirm port 3389 now gets allowed — then move that same rule to the very end (after default-deny) and confirm it becomes unreachable, directly demonstrating why rule order matters.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain why default-deny is safer than default-allow, why rule order matters in a firewall's rule list, and can articulate what network segmentation limits in the event of a breach.

checks.q: Why is a default-DENY firewall posture (block everything not explicitly allowed) generally considered safer than default-ALLOW (allow everything not explicitly blocked)?
checks.a: Default-deny only requires you to correctly list what SHOULD be allowed — anything you forgot to consider is safely blocked by default. Default-allow requires you to anticipate and explicitly block every possible bad case in advance, and anything you didn't think to block is left open, a much less reliable security posture.

keyTakeaways: A firewall evaluates rules in order, with the first match winning — a well-designed firewall ends with a default-deny rule.
Default-deny is safer than default-allow, since it only requires correctly listing what should be permitted rather than anticipating every bad case.
Network segmentation limits the blast radius of a breach — compromising one segment shouldn't automatically grant access to others.

topics.title: VPNs — extending a private, encrypted tunnel
topics.concept: A VPN (Virtual Private Network) creates an ENCRYPTED TUNNEL between your device and a VPN server, so traffic traveling over an untrusted network (like public WiFi) is protected from local eavesdropping — conceptually similar to the TLS encryption from the Cryptography module, but applied at the network level to ALL your traffic, not just one HTTPS connection. Critically, a VPN protects traffic BETWEEN you and the VPN server/endpoint — it does NOT make you anonymous to the destination website, and the VPN provider itself can see your traffic after it exits the tunnel, which is exactly why VPN provider trust/logging policy matters.
topics.analogy: Using the internet over public WiFi without a VPN is like having a conversation in a crowded room where anyone nearby can listen in. A VPN is like stepping into a soundproof phone booth connected by a private line to a trusted operator (the VPN server) — nobody in the room can hear you anymore, but the OPERATOR on the other end of that private line can still hear everything you say, and where your call gets routed to from there is entirely up to them — trusting the operator (the VPN provider) is just as important as the soundproofing itself.

examples.code:
# Illustrating the CONCEPT of what a VPN protects vs. doesn't -- not runnable network code,
# a conceptual model of the data path
without_vpn_path = [
    "Your device", "Public WiFi router (can see/intercept unencrypted traffic)",
    "ISP", "Destination website",
]
with_vpn_path = [
    "Your device", "[ENCRYPTED TUNNEL -- public WiFi router sees only encrypted noise]",
    "VPN server (traffic becomes visible again here)", "Destination website",
]

print("without VPN:", " -> ".join(without_vpn_path))
print("with VPN:   ", " -> ".join(with_vpn_path))
print("\nnotice: the VPN SERVER itself can see your traffic after the tunnel ends --")
print("a VPN shifts WHO can see your traffic, it doesn't eliminate visibility entirely")
examples.note: This is a WALKTHROUGH of the conceptual data path, not literal network code -- the key, often-missed point it illustrates: a VPN genuinely protects against LOCAL eavesdropping (the public WiFi router/ISP), but the VPN provider itself becomes the new party that can see your traffic, which is exactly why choosing a trustworthy VPN provider (and understanding their logging policy) matters just as much as using one at all.

topics.warn: A VPN is not the same as anonymity — the destination website can still see your activity (just from the VPN server's IP instead of yours), and the VPN provider can see your traffic after it exits the tunnel. Marketing claims of 'complete anonymity' from a VPN product should be treated skeptically against this real technical limitation.
mistakes: Assuming a VPN makes you completely anonymous online — it changes WHICH parties can see your traffic (shifting visibility from your local network to the VPN provider), it doesn't eliminate visibility altogether.
Choosing a VPN provider without considering their logging policy — since the VPN server CAN see your traffic after decryption, a provider that logs everything undermines much of the privacy benefit.

Assuming a VPN protects against everything a firewall or antivirus would — a VPN specifically protects the confidentiality of traffic in transit; it doesn't inspect content for malware or block malicious sites on its own.

topics.doneWhen: You can explain what a VPN actually protects (encrypted transit to the VPN server) versus what it does NOT provide (anonymity from the destination, or protection from the VPN provider itself).

checks.q: Does using a VPN prevent the destination website you visit from knowing your activity on that site?
checks.a: No — the destination website can still see and log your activity, just associated with the VPN server's IP address instead of your own. A VPN protects the confidentiality of your traffic IN TRANSIT (especially from local eavesdropping on the network between you and the VPN server), not your activity's visibility to the destination itself.

keyTakeaways: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and a VPN server, protecting traffic from local network eavesdropping.
A VPN does not provide anonymity — the destination site still sees your activity (from the VPN's IP), and the VPN provider can see your traffic after the tunnel ends.
A VPN provider's trustworthiness and logging policy matter as much as the encryption itself, since visibility shifts to them rather than disappearing.

topics.title: Man-in-the-middle attacks and ARP spoofing
topics.concept: A MAN-IN-THE-MIDDLE (MITM) attack secretly intercepts and potentially alters communication between two parties who believe they're talking directly to each other. ARP SPOOFING is a classic local-network MITM technique: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on a local network, but ARP has NO built-in authentication — any device can send an ARP reply CLAIMING to own any IP address, and other devices simply believe the most recent claim. An attacker exploits this by sending forged ARP replies claiming to be the router, redirecting victim traffic through the attacker's own machine.
topics.analogy: ARP is like a neighborhood where anyone can walk up and shout 'I'm the new resident at house #5' and everyone just updates their mental map to believe it — with no ID check whatsoever. An attacker exploiting this simply shouts 'I'm now the router' louder/more recently than the real router, and every neighbor's mail (network traffic) intended for the router starts getting delivered to the attacker's house instead, without anyone noticing anything looks different at first.

examples.code:
# Simulating the CONCEPT of ARP cache poisoning with a plain dictionary --
# a conceptual model, NOT a real network tool; never perform actual ARP spoofing
# against a network you don't own/control

arp_cache = {"192.168.1.1": "AA:AA:AA:AA:AA:AA"}   # the REAL router's MAC address
print("before attack -- arp_cache:", arp_cache)

# ARP has NO built-in authentication -- any device can claim to own any IP,
# and other devices simply believe the most recent claim
def receive_arp_reply(claimed_ip, claimed_mac, cache):
    cache[claimed_ip] = claimed_mac   # no verification happens here -- this IS the vulnerability

# An attacker (MAC BB:BB:BB:BB:BB:BB) sends a forged ARP reply claiming to BE the router
receive_arp_reply("192.168.1.1", "BB:BB:BB:BB:BB:BB", arp_cache)
print("after forged ARP reply -- arp_cache:", arp_cache)
print("\nthe victim device now sends router-bound traffic to the ATTACKER's MAC instead")
examples.note: Actually run and confirmed: the arp_cache dictionary is silently overwritten by the forged claim with zero verification -- this deliberately simple simulation captures the exact real vulnerability (ARP's total lack of authentication), which is the actual mechanism behind real ARP-spoofing tools, not just a metaphor.

topics.warn: Real ARP-spoofing tools exist and are genuinely capable of this attack on a real network — never run one against any network you don't own or have explicit written authorization to test. This lesson's example is a pure conceptual simulation using a plain Python dictionary, never touching a real network interface.
mistakes: Assuming HTTPS alone fully protects against MITM concerns on a local network — HTTPS (via TLS, from the Cryptography module) DOES protect the content of properly-verified connections even over an ARP-spoofed path, which is exactly why certificate verification matters so much; but non-HTTPS traffic on the same network remains fully exposed to an ARP-spoofing MITM.

Thinking MITM attacks require sophisticated tools — ARP spoofing exploits a fundamental protocol design gap (no authentication) that's been well-understood for decades; the barrier is authorization and ethics, not technical difficulty.

Confusing ARP spoofing (a local-network-only attack, since ARP doesn't route beyond your local network segment) with attacks that work across the wider internet — this is specifically why network segmentation (previous lesson) limits ARP-spoofing's blast radius to one local segment.
topics.handsOn: Run the example and confirm the ARP cache is silently overwritten with the forged entry. Then research (via the resource below) one real, standard defense against ARP spoofing (e.g. static ARP entries, or switch-level Dynamic ARP Inspection) and explain in one sentence how it addresses the specific lack-of-authentication gap this lesson demonstrates.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what a man-in-the-middle attack is, how ARP spoofing specifically exploits ARP's lack of authentication, and why HTTPS/TLS still matters even on a network vulnerable to ARP spoofing.

checks.q: Why does ARP spoofing work at all — what specific weakness in the ARP protocol does it exploit?
checks.a: ARP has no built-in authentication mechanism — any device on the local network can send an ARP reply claiming to own any IP address, and other devices simply trust and update their cache with the most recent claim, with no way to verify the claim is genuine.

keyTakeaways: A man-in-the-middle attack secretly intercepts communication between two parties who believe they're talking directly to each other.
ARP spoofing exploits ARP's complete lack of built-in authentication — any device can falsely claim to own any IP address on the local network.
HTTPS/TLS's certificate verification (Cryptography module) still protects properly-verified connections even over an ARP-spoofed network path, which is exactly why it matters.

topics.title: Network scanning — from a single port check to real tooling
topics.concept: Module 1's single-port check extends naturally into scanning a RANGE of ports efficiently (using concurrent connections, since checking hundreds of ports one at a time would be slow) — exactly what a real scanning tool does at a larger scale. NMAP is the industry-standard network scanning tool: `nmap -p <ports> <target>` scans specific ports, `-sV` additionally probes open ports to identify the actual SERVICE/VERSION running, and `-sn` does host-discovery only (no port scan) — and nmap's own project explicitly provides `scanme.nmap.org` as a genuinely authorized, legal practice target specifically for learning the tool.
topics.analogy: Module 1's single check_port() call is like knocking on one specific apartment door and waiting to see if anyone answers. A real scanner (or nmap) is like a building inspector systematically and efficiently knocking on every apartment door in parallel, noting which ones answer (open ports) — and `-sV` is that same inspector asking a follow-up question at each answered door ('what's your job title?') to identify not just THAT something is there, but WHAT it actually is.

examples.code:
import socket
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def check_port(host, port, timeout=0.5):
    sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    sock.settimeout(timeout)
    result = sock.connect_ex((host, port))
    sock.close()
    return port, result == 0

def scan_range(host, ports):
    open_ports = []
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=50) as executor:
        results = executor.map(lambda p: check_port(host, p), ports)
        for port, is_open in results:
            if is_open:
                open_ports.append(port)
    return sorted(open_ports)

# Scanning YOUR OWN localhost -- always authorized
common_ports = [21, 22, 23, 25, 53, 80, 443, 3306, 3389, 5432, 8080]
open_ports = scan_range("127.0.0.1", common_ports)
print(f"scanned {len(common_ports)} common ports on localhost")
print(f"open ports found: {open_ports}")

mistakes: Scanning any host other than your own systems or an explicitly authorized target like scanme.nmap.org — even a 'harmless' scan of a random website is unauthorized network scanning.

Running an intensive nmap scan against scanme.nmap.org more than the courtesy limit nmap's own docs request (roughly a dozen scans per day) — it's a free, shared service maintained for the community's benefit.

Assuming a fast concurrent scan (or an aggressive nmap scan) is always the right approach — a real, high-volume scan against production infrastructure (even your own) can cause real load/disruption; scan thoughtfully, not just quickly.

checks.a: The nmap project itself explicitly and publicly states permission to scan scanme.nmap.org, specifically for practicing with the nmap tool (though not for testing exploits or denial-of-service). A random website has given no such authorization, so scanning it — even non-destructively — would be unauthorized activity.

keyTakeaways: A concurrent port scanner (checking many ports in parallel) is dramatically faster than checking ports one at a time, the same principle real scanning tools use at scale.
nmap's -p scans specific ports, -sV identifies service/version info on open ports, and -sn does host discovery only.
scanme.nmap.org is nmap's own explicitly authorized practice target — a genuine, legal option for hands-on scanning practice.
